claims.text: Rapid solidification of Co-free FeNiCrMn forms nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates.
Nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates impede dislocation motion in as-solidified FeNiCrMn.
Nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates delay dynamic recrystallization in as-solidified FeNiCrMn.
Precipitate-controlled deformation preserves a favorable strength–ductility balance across a wide range of temperatures and strain rates.
The initial as-solidified FeNiCrMn has a fine, homogeneous grain structure.
The initial as-solidified FeNiCrMn has a uniform distribution of nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates.
Rapidly solidified FeNiCrMn has a high initial dislocation density.
Dynamic mechanical tests will span approximately 25–900 °C and multiple strain rates.
Controlled atmospheres and comparable rapid-solidification processing will be used to limit differences in initial microstructure.
Post-solidification heat treatment can dissolve or coarsen the Mn-based oxide precipitates while retaining the base composition.
The nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates produce Orowan strengthening.
The nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates exert Zener drag on migrating grain boundaries.
Between 25 and 600 °C, the precipitates obstruct dislocation glide and favor slip or twinning mechanisms.
At temperatures of at least 700 °C, the precipitates impede grain-boundary migration and delay dynamic recrystallization.
Delayed dynamic recrystallization sustains dislocation-forest hardening and overall strength.

As-solidified material retaining nanoscale precipitates will have higher yield strength and a better-preserved strength–ductility balance than heat-treated material with reduced or coarsened precipitates.
Precipitate-retaining material will show a delayed onset of dynamic recrystallization relative to heat-treated material.
The proposed mechanism is limited to FeNiCrMn produced under similar rapid-solidification conditions and may not apply to material with substantially different defects or impurity levels.
TEM, SEM, and EBSD measurements will relate precipitate state, dislocation density, grain size, and recrystallized fraction to stress–strain behavior.
The hypothesis is falsified if reducing or coarsening the precipitates leaves the strength–ductility response and dynamic-recrystallization onset effectively unchanged.
